title: Draper’s Long Road Back: Injury, a Ranking Plunge, and Now a Murray-Guided Return
summary: Jack Draper’s career has been a study in cruel timing. In an 18-month burst, the 24-year-old reached a US Open semifinal, cracked the top five, and won the prestigious Indian Wells title. Then his body betrayed him. A bone bruise in his serving arm sidelined him for nearly seven months. He returned in February, only to injure his knee in Barcelona in early April. The result: just 11 matches in a year and a ranking freefall from No. 4 to No. 113. Now, Draper is staging his latest comeback at Eastbourne next week — and he’ll have a new voice in his corner. In a surprise move last month, Draper parted with coach Jamie Delgado and brought in Andy Murray, the three-time Grand Slam champion who knows a thing or two about comebacks. Murray, 39, has been working with Draper at the National Tennis Centre in London and likes what he sees. “I’ve been incredibly impressed with his tennis on the practice court,” Murray said. “He’s a super quick learner and a brilliant player.” The partnership’s immediate goal is simple: get Draper match-tough before Wimbledon starts on June 29. “The number one priority is getting him back on the match court, competing and gaining trust in his body again,” Murray said. Whether this becomes a long-term project remains to be seen, but for a player once seen as Britain’s next leading man, having Murray in his corner feels like a crucial reset. Meanwhile, Emma Raducanu has opted to skip Eastbourne and will prepare for Wimbledon on the practice courts after reaching the Queen’s final last week.
why_it_matters: Draper's story shows that even the brightest talents can have their careers nearly destroyed by injuries. For a teenager, this is a powerful lesson in resilience and in how asking for help—from someone like Murray who survived worse—can be the smartest move.

background_read: Jack Draper burst onto the tennis scene in 2024, reaching the semi‑finals of the US Open, one of the four Grand Slam tournaments. He then won the Indian Wells Masters 1000 title, which is considered the most important tournament after the Slams.

Andy Murray (a three‑time Grand Slam champion from Britain) famously battled a career‑threatening hip injury for years before finally having surgery. His own experiences make him uniquely qualified to guide a player facing injury problems.
The National Tennis Centre in London is the headquarters of British tennis, where top players train with elite coaches, physiotherapists and fitness experts.

The world rankings in tennis are calculated from a player's best total points over the past 52 weeks. A long injury lay‑off often causes a sudden ranking crash because earlier points expire and cannot be replaced.

perspectives.description: Having Andy Murray in his corner is a huge advantage. Murray understands the physical and mental pain of returning from serious injury and can offer practical advice no textbook can. If Draper stays healthy, this partnership could bring him back to the top 10.

Rushing back too quickly after repeated bone and knee problems could make things worse. There is a real danger that Draper's body simply cannot handle the grind of the ATP Tour, and another setback might end his career entirely.

Professional tennis is brutal on the body. Many top‑50 players go through cycles of injury, ranking collapse and recovery. Draper’s case fits a well‑known pattern; what makes it unusual is that he is trying to shortcut the recovery by leaning on a recently retired legend.

If Murray can successfully guide Draper back to the top, it could start a trend of recently retired players becoming full‑time coaches for broken stars. Tennis might see a generation of players whose second act is coaching, reshaping how injury comebacks are managed.
